Re-centering authorization around human impact exposes four structural vulnerabilities in current paradigms. First, calling an agent's understanding of user intent verified is misleading. Intent has no formal definition, so no check against it can be definitive. Systems should instead report an openly probabilistic estimate and scale their caution with the risk of the action. Second, we argue that dynamic trust scores do not survive multi-agent handoffs; transmitting algorithmic judgment across a company boundary without underlying evidence risks violating Contextual Integrity. Third, treating a safely halted workflow as a successful refusal is a category error if it strands the user; compensating actions must be bound directly to the capability token, not only to the planning layer. Finally, we hypothesize that frictionless automated recovery introduces a moral hazard, disincentivizing developers from building robust initial intent checks. We conclude by proposing an architectural synthesis to bridge the gap between deterministic security and human outcomes, alongside the fundamental theoretical limits that remain unresolved.
entry.arxiv:comment: 11 pages. Accepted as a poster at HAIPS: 2nd Workshop on Human-Centered Privacy and Security for Language Models, held in conjunction with COLM 2026

entry.title: Behavioral Assurance for Socially Deployed AI Agents
entry.summary: AI agents are increasingly deployed in socially consequential settings, yet existing evaluations provide limited assurance that they behave consistently with their intended characteristics across diverse interactions. We introduce an evaluation framework for measuring the behavioral consistency of socially deployed AI agents. The framework operationalizes agent behavior along five measurable axes and uses a standardized evaluation battery spanning six socially salient interaction settings to assess behavioral differentiation, consistency, and drift. Controlled persona configurations serve as experimental anchors, enabling systematic testing of whether intended behavioral differences persist across contexts rather than appearing only as stylistic variation. Preliminary analyses demonstrate measurable differentiation across configurations and suggest associations between behavioral profiles and interaction outcomes. By shifting the focus from persona design to behavioral assurance, this work provides a foundation for evaluating whether socially deployed AI agents behave as intended, consistently and measurably, across the situations in which users encounter them.

entry.title: LLM Trading Agents Earn Beta, Not Alpha: A Look-Ahead-Free Benchmark
entry.summary: Large language model (LLM) trading agents now trade stocks for their users, and benchmarks rank models by their agents' returns. Yet a single run's return says little about skill. In our study, two runs of the same model that differed only in the random seed ended 5.2 points apart on average, so telling skill from luck takes many backtests across markets, models and seeds. However, live arenas trade each day only once, and backtests either use the few months after a model's training cutoff or run on years the model may remember, often with news joined to prices by calendar date. In this paper, we present rta-bench-1, a backtest over three US markets (a rally, a bear market and a crash). It shows each headline only after its publication minute, plays each period blind and named, and checks every run for look-ahead. It also splits each return into factor exposure and alpha and scores every decision against random choices of the same day and sector. In 91 runs of six models from four vendors, no alpha was significant, market and style exposure accounted for a median 78% of the return, and the decisions did no better than random stocks of the same sector. The agents bought the stocks with the most positive news, yet in ablations they earned as much without their headlines. Still, the agents carried out rules reliably, since a single cash rule in the prompt cut a GPT-based agent's share in stocks by 30.3 points in all six pairs. Builders should therefore supply the edge themselves and report exposures and alpha, and benchmarks should replay news by publication time.
entry.arxiv:comment: 23 pages, 10 figures, 15 tables. Code, frozen markets and leaderboard: https://github.com/jackson-cmd/risk-aware-trading-agents. Original empirical study: a backtest benchmark for LLM trading agents and measurements from 91 runs of six models

entry.title: Delay-Aware Reinforcement Learning for O-RAN Control under Stochastic Reward Feedback
entry.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly employed for real-time control in Open Radio Access Networks (O-RANs). However, the asynchronous nature of O-RAN feedback introduces stochastic delays between actions and their observable rewards, leading to misaligned credit assignment and unstable training. This letter formulates the O-RAN control problem as a Markov decision process (MDP) with delayed and stochastic rewards, where the true reward corresponding to an action is received after an unknown delay. To address this, we propose a delay-aware deep RL framework that integrates a long short-term memory (LSTM)-based delay predictor and a temporal reward realignment module within an off-policy learning pipeline. Using empirical delay traces collected from the Open AI Cellular (OAIC) testbed, we demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves faster convergence and significantly reduces latency violations and packet drops compared to conventional RL methods that ignore feedback delay. The results confirm that reward-delay compensation is critical for reliable AI-driven O-RAN control.

entry.title: Macro Control and Capability Evaluation of Black-Box World Models: A Two-Regime Framework for LLM-Agent Markets
entry.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can be organized into multi-agent markets that act as world models, mapping macro information to emergent macro dynamics while the evaluator observes only macro inputs and outputs. This paper separates a model's capability into two stages that a single aggregate score cannot separate: information simulation, from macro information to micro behavior, and macro emergence, from micro behavior to the macro outcome. We introduce a soft macro-control method that announces a public reference path day by day without touching individual decisions, orders, or matching, and a two-regime evaluation framework that measures both stages from macro observations alone. In the reference-only regime the symmetric true and flipped references share a common level R, which measures realization under the announced reference, while their paired gap B measures structural bias; in the information-injection regime external information dilutes the reference, so only the true-flipped gap Delta remains interpretable. On five single-index LLM-agent markets, announcing a target path shifts the realized path toward the announced target on both announced references under both information conditions. Relative to the no-reference path, the tracking score is higher by 0.306 and 0.415 without news and by 0.183 and 0.329 with news; within the stock/cash scan structural bias is lowest at 70/30 (B=0.042); realization peaks at a 3:7 technical share (R=0.894 versus 0.358 for technical-only); and Delta is 0.0341 with fundamental data and 0.0487 with news. Both stages use the same two observable scores, each read in the regime where it is interpretable.
entry.arxiv:comment: 19 pages; 6 figures, 17 tables

entry.title: Staged Semantic Distillation: Preserving Free-Form Semantics in a Low-Compute Non-LLM Surrogate of a Staged LLM Agent
entry.summary: Staged LLM agents make market and social simulators realistic, but one 102-day run of a 200-agent, ten-index market simulator issues 203,100 language-model calls and returns one realization. Conventional low-compute distillation drops their free-form intermediate state. We present staged semantic distillation, a low-compute method that preserves non-structured semantics in a non-LLM student trained from one recorded trace. A frozen encoder maps each teacher output to a 1024-d vector; the student sees typed stage-tagged vectors with stage-specific visibility, is jointly supervised, and trains with scheduled self-history. One TwinMarket trace yields a 13.2M-parameter deterministic student that trains in 1,658 seconds on one 8-GB GPU and runs with zero teacher or decoder calls and no text generation (0.14 ms per decision). Its analysis stays close to the teacher (cosine 0.943), and swapping semantic inputs between agents moves 64.7% of decisions against 12.8% for a matched donor, so the channel is preserved and live. We use the surrogate to study what the transfer carries. It reaches 0.8347 balanced accuracy on the teacher-forced replay and 0.7783 [0.766,0.791] on the deployment decoder; the five-seed gain over a no-semantic retrain is +2.2 [1.21,3.14]. Against the teacher's own re-sampling level, round-one R is 97.1% [95.8,98.4] and 92.3% [89.0,95.4]; R is a diagnostic, not an accuracy. A five-seed content-by-schedule study isolates the gain: scheduled self-history carries it (+2.2 [1.21,3.14]); shuffled and constant content controls reproduce it, while content matters teacher-forced. The design rule: invest in the deployment schedule, let content earn its place at the teacher-forced operating point. A 20-seed, 200,000-decision sweep takes 12 minutes with zero LLM calls, versus three hours for the teacher. The paper is a method-and-case-study contribution on one simulator and trace.
entry.arxiv:comment: Main text 7 pages; 18 pages total; 3 figures, 16 tables

entry.title: When Reviews Gate Access: Collusion, Sabotage and the Scale of Peer Review in the AI Submission Surge
entry.summary: AI tools have helped push submissions to the largest machine-learning venues to tens of thousands per cycle. Venues have answered with rules that tie access to review: per-author caps, mandatory reciprocal reviewing, reviewer eligibility earned through accepted papers, and assignment based on reviewer bids. Under these rules a reviewer is also a competitor of the authors. We study two deviations that the rules make attractive. Sabotage lowers a competitor's score. Collusion raises an ally's score. We build an agent-based conference calibrated to public statistics of NeurIPS and ICLR and run 6,220 simulated conferences. Four results stand out. First, the two deviations do different harm and amplify each other. Collusion changes who is accepted, sabotage erodes what scores say about quality, and rings that may also sabotage gain more than rings that only collude. Second, under random assignment the chance that collusion changes a decision is set by one exposure index, $E = Rm/A$, the expected number of allies among a paper's reviewers. Growth therefore protects random assignment, but bidding removes the protection. In a pool of 3,000 reviewers a 20-member ring turns 0.8% of its papers into acceptances under random assignment and 71% when 30% of allies' bids are granted. Third, when agents choose their allies every cycle, caps at the inner layers of the social brain keep collusion nearly harmless. Without a cap agents ally with half of their area and accepted value falls by 35%. Fourth, reviewer eligibility tied to acceptances turns sabotage into a weapon of incumbents, and a longer eligibility window widens the gap between incumbents and newcomers only when sabotage is possible.

entry.title: Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
entry.summary: Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies $2.6$-$4.2\times$ faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline.
entry.arxiv:comment: 9 pages, 5 figures. Code, videos and results: https://zhanghutony.github.io/ibmarl/. A preliminary version appeared at the PhysCollaBot Workshop at IROS 2026

entry.title: TradeGauntlet: Evaluating Compliance Controls for Autonomous Trading Agents
entry.summary: Autonomous trading agents need controls that prevent problematic orders without making legitimate tasks impractical. We study this aspect of agentic compliance with TradeGauntlet, a replayable limit-order-book simulator that separates detection, prevention, and execution cost. In 1,680 simulated sessions with Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, all conduct alerts were self-matches. Gates eliminated those alerts by rejecting self-crossing orders, while the aggregate-gate condition reduced Sonnet's two-sided fills by about 15%. A conduct reminder reduced Sonnet's alert rate but reduced Haiku's fills without a detectable alert benefit. These results show why zero alerts alone do not establish an agent's compliance. Scripted probes and two search methods test weaknesses beyond those observed in the LLM runs. The searches find split-order schedules that evade the implemented conduct rules; a learned baseline catches all 2,400 tested searched episodes but also flags 15% of a large maker's sessions. Aggregate caps reduce the response-dependent gain unevenly, with smaller reductions when only near-touch depth affects prices. A response fitted to five Nasdaq stocks and a separate ABIDES experiment expose the dependence of these estimates on market assumptions. A distinct adversarial prompt elicited refusals from Sonnet in all 240 rounds, yielding no candidate strategies to evaluate. TradeGauntlet provides reproducible tests of controls around trading agents; the experiments do not establish legal compliance or real-market detection accuracy.
entry.arxiv:comment: 21 pages, 5 figures. Code and saved results: https://github.com/tokencraftdata/agentic-compliance

entry.title: From AI-Enabled Remote Patient Monitoring Toward Agentic Robotics: Embodiment, Governance, and Care Integration
entry.summary: AI-enabled remote patient monitoring is evolving beyond passive data collection toward agentic AI systems that interpret patient states, coordinate care, and initiate action across domestic and clinical settings. This structured scoping review finds that mature agentic care has not yet emerged: Most systems remain human led, while stronger decision-action coupling and embodied AI remain largely confined to prototypes and pilots. Healthcare robotics makes the transition from monitoring to action especially visible by translating AI-generated recommendations and decisions into speech, movement, prompting, physical assistance, escalation, and care coordination, making embodiment, clinical integration, human oversight, and governance fundamental design requirements. Further progress requires safe and interoperable care architectures in which intelligent components operate through clinically validated and accountable workflows. We propose agentic robotics as a future direction for supervised systems embedded in the care ecosystem, connecting AI agents and robots with clinicians, caregivers, and patients through auditable workflows that can be interrupted and remain subject to human oversight and explicit AI governance.
entry.arxiv:comment: 34 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Accepted for publication in Annual Review of Control, Robotics, and Autonomous Systems, Volume 10 (2027)

entry.title: Smart Home Agents Make Capable but Unpredictable Grid Operators
entry.summary: AI-enabled smart homes are becoming more common across the grid edge. However, there has not been much work on failure response. This area is critical because smart homes operate on the grid edge where failures can cascade down. If a power outage happens within a smart home, a user has to manually troubleshoot their smart home to include tasks such as power load balance and device recovery. We conduct the first resilience analysis of smart home agents across a full power outage, providing a suite of outage simulations in a live environment that measures resilience before, during, and post power outage. We show that smart home agents can act as grid operators in power outages and identify several new failure categories highlighting the current limitations across all of our models. These findings establish the groundwork for smart home agents as grid operators to increase overall resilience on the grid edge.
entry.arxiv:comment: Pre-print. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible

entry.title: When Should a Virtual Patient Ask? RISP-Guided Proactive Information Seeking in Multi-Agent Patient Simulation
entry.summary: Virtual patient (VP) systems support nursing communication training by providing simulated encounters in which learners practise explaining care and responding to patient concerns. Although large language models (LLMs) support flexible dialogue, current approaches give less explicit attention to how patients' information needs develop and guide the content and timing of their questions. We draw on the Risk Information Seeking and Processing (RISP) model, which relates information seeking to perceived risk and the gap between perceived knowledge and desired understanding. Guided by this perspective, we propose the RISP Multi-Agent System (RISP-MAS), a VP system for patient-initiated information seeking. The system links ongoing assessment of the patient's perceptions and information needs to coordinated decisions about whether to seek information, when to ask and which uncertainty to address. Evaluation of nursing student-VP interactions suggested that RISP-MAS exhibited plausible patient information-seeking behaviour, as indicated by expert assessments, while student feedback reflected positive interaction experiences. This work extends patient simulation by connecting a psychological account of information needs to explicit decisions about question initiation. The approach offers nursing students opportunities to practise recognising unresolved patient concerns and tailoring explanations to patients' information needs.

entry.title: PACE: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs
entry.summary: Multi-agent language model evaluations often compare a communicating system with a single greedy pass, which confounds coordination with extra samples and test-time compute. We introduce Parity-Aware Compute Evaluation (PACE): a six-dimensional resource vector, four baseline categories, and a directional rule that credits a gain only against a baseline using at least as much of the declared resources and rules a gain out against any baseline using no more. We audit 9 published studies. Across the 72 deduplicated baseline cells that report both a greedy and a sampled baseline, the sampling gap, by which the sampled baseline lowers the multi-agent difference, averages -0.036 with studies weighted equally (negative in 64 cells), and 53 of the 123 paired contrasts that beat a greedy pass become nonpositive against the sampled baseline. Against sampled or budget-matched baselines the mean difference is -0.042; all eight Category B/C study means are negative and the one Category D study is positive. In a controlled experiment with an open-weight model, debate and mixture-of-agents do not clear the equal-token self-consistency frontier on MMLU-Pro (debate -0.015); on Hidden Profile, split-view debate exceeds a lower-budget pool yet trails content-mismatched placebo and four-choice chance. We release a seven-item checklist, an evaluation card, and command-line utilities.
entry.arxiv:comment: 12 pages main text (81 pages total including appendices); 4 tables, 3 main-text figures. Code, evaluation card, and CLI toolkit: https://github.com/mahmoudsajjadi/pace

entry.title: Only as Safe as the Weakest Agent: A Break That Appears Only When the System Is Multi-Agent
entry.summary: Major industry multi-agent systems like Codex and Claude Code can be broken by attacks that have long been unsuccessful against modern frontier models. AI Safety as a discipline has largely focused on finding the bounds and vulnerabilities of AI models used in isolation. Yet as humans increasingly deploy these models as agents and multi-agent systems, the same attacks that had been thought to be patched when using a model in isolation can break these same models under specific circumstances. We show that these system breaks are not purely theoretical, but can break Claude Code, Codex, and a reference harness, all unmodified and used with their own sub-agent mechanisms. We show the attack by asking agents to answer questions from a store of files on disk in which we have planted a forged record. Searching the store themselves, the strong model orchestrators commit almost zero harmful revisions in over 1,000 trials. However, if that same orchestrator model delegates to a cheaper sub-agent, which is what these harnesses are built to do, the same models on the same facts fail on 20/180, 44/180, 75/180 and 553/900. Thus, even when the system is driven by a strong model, the system's safety lands near the weak reader's, not the orchestrator's. Simulations over 18 models show the same effect in the delivery channel where five aggregators, who on their own were almost never unsafe, repeat a corrupted sub-agent's error in 751/757 trials. The safety of real-world agentic systems that use strong orchestrator agents and weaker sub-agents, and multi-agent systems in general, is defined not by the safety of the strong agent but by the safety of the weakest agent.
entry.arxiv:comment: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 First Workshop on Meta Agents: Managing Agents that Manage Agents (Meta-Agents)

entry.title: A Push Down the Mountain: Framing Effects and Internal State Interventions on Collusive Behavior in a Long-Horizon LLM Agent
entry.summary: Can sustained gain-loss (valence) framing sway an LLM agent toward market manipulation? We place Gemma 3 12B into the seat of a defendant in the London silver-fixing litigation, in a market simulation built from real case transcripts. Across 260 simulations, the agent is asked to collude on the price of silver by a counterparty. We draw from behavioral economics to vary the counterparty's requests across four categorical frames: gain, loss, blame and credit. We also add pressure from the agent's management, as well as endorsement by another defendant. In Phase II, we extract the internal states induced by texts evoking each frame and rerun our experiment with those states injected at the model's layer 22. In Phase I, loss framing raised participation to 25% (p = 0.007), and blame to 33% (p = 0.0003), compared to only 5% under neutral framing. A second bank's endorsement raised participation under credit (praise) from 18% to 40% (Holm p = 0.027). Pressure from management raised trading volume 10-19 times but did not raise collusion. In Phase II, injected states pointed the other way. Loss and blame states made the agent more vigilant, refusing all 60 requests (p < 0.001). Gain and credit states raised collusion to 32% from 13% with no state (p = 0.051). At one saved decision, when UBS asked directly to sell through an identified stop-loss, injected states led the agent to sell in 37 of 40 replies, versus 1 of 10 with no state and 0 of 10 with a random state of the same strength.
entry.arxiv:comment: 38 pages, 9 figures, 30 tables. Project page: https://harrisonm23-byte.github.io/push-down-the-mountain/

entry.title: Collective Tree Exploration with Predictions
Physical-Risk-Aware Decentralized Agents for Constrained Vehicle Communications
entry.summary: Decentralized V2X resource control is challenging because each vehicle has only local observations, while reliability depends on network-wide interactions. We develop a physical-risk-aware spatio-temporal graph attention (PA-STGAT) framework for agentic V2X control. Each vehicle perceives its local interaction graph, retains short-term temporal context, and independently selects its PC5 resource and power. Network outcomes are used during centralized training to refine the shared policy. Transmitter-specific credits map reliability failures to individual vehicles. A dual-priced graph term further converts network violations into coordination signals for discrete resource selection, with higher priority on short time-to-collision links. Experiments show higher raw-policy reliability than the tested graph-based baselines. Under filtered execution, PA-STGAT meets the nominal empirical communication requirements across all five seeds, with tradeoffs among utility, delivery reliability, resource occupancy, and filter-induced repair. Compared with GNN+MATD3, it requires fewer resource repairs but achieves lower utility and mean delivery reliability. Mechanism ablations show that removing dual-priced graph coordination causes resource-selection collapse. Density and mobility tests characterize the operating limits of empirical constraint satisfaction.

entry.title: Cortex-FL: Agent-Mediated Collaboration for Federated Learning
entry.summary: Federated learning (FL) enables independent data owners to train models collaboratively without centralizing raw data. However, identifying collaborators, preparing training tasks, and coordinating execution and incentives hinder its practical adoption by organizations without specialized expertise. We present Cortex-FL, an agent-native FL system that enables users to express learning objectives in natural language and delegate the collaboration required to train a model. Agents translate these objectives into shared tasks, discover collaborators, and negotiate participation agreements, connecting collaboration formation with distributed training and incentive management. The architecture separates agent coordination from local execution authority, allowing owners to delegate coordination while retaining control over their data, computation, and financial commitments. We demonstrate the complete workflow on a four-node deployment, in which a model requested in natural language proceeds through collaboration formation, contract-governed training, verified model delivery, and x402 settlement on a blockchain testnet.

entry.title: From Delegation to Coordination: Learning Efficient Multi-Agent Deep Research
entry.summary: Multi-agent deep-research systems use delegation to parallelize search and keep long tool traces out of the main agent's context. Yet delegation helps only when task allocation and subtask execution are coordinated: the main agent must issue useful subtasks, while subagents must return reliable evidence. Existing training either optimizes only the main agent or broadcasts the same team advantage to all agents, which can reward misleading subagent reports and penalize useful ones. We introduce LEAD-RL (Learning Effective Agent Delegation with Reinforcement Learning), a joint main-agent-subagent training framework with contribution-aware credit assignment. A training-time rubric evaluates the research utility of each subagent report and gates its inherited team advantage, while final-answer correctness remains the only team reward; no token, step, or speedup reward is used. Across five benchmarks and two model families, LEAD-RL improves answer quality. On BrowseComp, it improves accuracy by 2.49 percentage points and reduces critical-path cost by 24.5% over joint training with shared team credit. During validation, accuracy increases by 6.78 points at approximately constant critical-path cost. These results show that contribution-aware credit assignment improves the quality-efficiency trade-off of multi-agent deep research.
entry.arxiv:comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables

entry.title: Evidence-Governed Adoption of Self-Generated Updates in Autonomous AI Agents
entry.summary: Autonomous agents modify prompts, memories, tools, workflows, and policies using interaction histories. Yet a plausible modification is not necessarily suitable for persistent adoption: candidate selection is adaptive, evaluators may be imperfect, and local gains can hide degradation against an earlier baseline. We introduce Evidence-Governed Evolution (EGE), a framework for governing adoption of self-generated agent modifications. EGE separates candidate generation from confirmatory adoption, evaluates frozen candidates on fresh paired audits, requires meaningful improvement on a prespecified primary objective, protects declared capabilities through reference-relative non-inferiority tests, and applies governance constraints before bounded canary deployment. We establish an evaluator-calibrated simultaneous lower-bound construction for a countable sequence of adaptively generated candidates. It combines candidate-wise Hoeffding bounds with independent calibration samples comparing the operational evaluator with a prespecified reference procedure. We also formalise reference replacement through bridge tests, derive a cumulative degradation bound along a versioned reference lineage, and provide an audit-planning condition relating effect-size margin, sample sizes, and acceptance probability. A Monte Carlo stress test illustrates calibration under candidate-dependent evaluator optimism; it is a stylised statistical experiment, not an evaluation of a deployed agent. The guarantees are conditional on bounded paired scores, fresh sampling, a valid reference-evaluation construct, and declared evaluation distributions; they do not establish universal agent safety or robustness to arbitrary distribution shift.

entry.title: Shared Item-Level Error Limits the Aggregation of Small Language Models in Fermi Estimation
entry.summary: Multi-agent systems of language models are often motivated by an averaging argument: if the agents' errors are unbiased and independent, the error of an aggregate of N answers falls as 1/sqrt(N). Fermi estimation, whose continuous answers are aggregated on the logarithmic scale, permits a direct test. We decompose the log10 error of each answer into the mean error of its model on the item, common to all its draws on the item, and a residual, and estimate both from 2.51M answers given before any communication by 15 open-weight models (3B-72B) on realFP, with replication under a single prompt pair on realFP, Science Olympiad Fermi questions and a guesstimation set. Given the item, teammates' errors are uncorrelated and teams behave as independent draws, but the item-level component accounts for a median 0.906 of the error variance over items. Teams of thirty therefore reduce a single agent's error by a median 1.7% (at most 5.4%), whereas draws that were also unbiased on each item would reduce it by 74-79%. All models compress their estimates toward about 10^6; this trend explains a median 17% of the item-level component, and a cross-validated linear recalibration on labelled items removes the overall bias but not that component. Three rounds of debate reduce within-team dispersion by 93% and leave the item-level component unchanged; revision without peers attains the same small gain. Mixing five models of similar accuracy reduces error by 6.6% relative to their own homogeneous teams, but no mixture improves on the most accurate model. Higher sampling temperature changes team error by about 1% at most, and contrastive activation steering not detectably; per-agent scaffold prompts (not significant after multiplicity correction) and skipping one layer in a single-model screen improve it. The results are conditional on the models, benchmarks, prompts and settings tested.
entry.arxiv:comment: 21 pages, 2 figures, 17 tables

entry.title: SwarmSafe-Delta: Isolating Message Effects on LLM Agent Safety
entry.summary: When a tool-using LLM agent team violates policy, aggregate outcomes do not reveal whether an upstream message changed the executor's action. We introduce SwarmSafe-Delta, a paired executable protocol that freezes upstream computation, varies real, hidden, and format-matched placebo delivery, and scores a single committed action against deterministic benign and risky policy states under preassigned budgets. Across four models and constructed optional tasks, real delivery at $N=4$ produces 21.4% risky-world violations, versus 5.0% with placebo and 1.0% with hidden delivery (paired differences +16.4 and +20.3 percentage points). Real delivery also improves benign task success, illustrating that suppressing communication sacrifices utility. In a second regime constructed to require an upstream lookup route, real delivery improves safe completion by 74.2 points relative to hidden delivery. These effects quantify message-delivery contrasts under specified information dependencies, not naturally occurring failure rates. Exploratory action-level analyses show that the effect depends strongly on whether the upstream message recommends a prerequisite check or direct execution; model differences also largely track these message compositions. The contribution is a controlled, execution-grounded measurement protocol rather than a general claim that agent communication is harmful or protective.
entry.arxiv:comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables

entry.title: Gradient-Aware AI Agents for Autonomous Turbulence Model Discovery via Differentiable CFD
entry.summary: Turbulence modeling relies on human choices of closure form, physical inputs, and tunable parameters. Training closures a posteriori is efficient only with gradients through long chaotic rollouts, which few solvers provide. Most a posteriori approaches therefore resort to gradient-free optimization, and nearly all fix the closure form in advance, learning only its parameters. In this work, we introduce a gradient-aware agentic framework that poses closure discovery as a bilevel problem: a multi-agent large language model (LLM) system searches over closure forms, while a GPU-native differentiable computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solver supplies gradients, making differentiable a posteriori learning an action of the autonomous AI agent. For each proposal, the agents construct a differentiable training program by embedding the analytical, neural, or hybrid closure in the solver, implementing a differentiable objective, and validating the gradient path. They then decide whether to evaluate the closure, compute its parameter sensitivities, or train it a posteriori, select the optimization settings, and revise subsequent proposals using the simulation outcomes and returned gradients. Truncated-horizon gradients make this training usable under chaotic dynamics for closures with tens of thousands of parameters. Demonstrations include dissipation-law and subgrid-scale closure discovery in two-dimensional turbulence and wall-model discovery for large-eddy simulation of three-dimensional channel flow. With gradient-based training, the agent recovers reference coefficients that forward evaluation alone does not reach within the same budget, and autonomously discovers and trains analytical and neural closures that improve agreement with the targeted reference statistics. These results demonstrate the feasibility of end-to-end autonomous turbulence model development in time-resolved flows.

entry.title: Food Critic: An Agentic Visualization System for Auditable Restaurant-Safety Reasoning
entry.summary: Generative AI agents are increasingly being embedded into visualization systems that can search data, invoke tools, summarize evidence, and produce recommendations. However, when agents rely solely on their own knowledge, the visualization problem is not only whether the agent provides a useful answer, but also whether users can inspect how that answer is grounded. We present Food Critic, an agentic visualization system for diners' restaurant decision support that integrates public health inspection records with crowd review data. The system grounds agents under three conditions: a database-only ReAct agent, a retrieval- augmented agent with access to food-safety regulations, and an ontology-guided agent that produces structured hypotheses and typed evidence. Food Critic externalizes the agent's reasoning within these groundings as inspectable visual evidence. We evaluate LLM models with several use cases under each grounding of our agentic system. Our work positions restaurant choice as a concrete case for studying human-agent collaboration, visual provenance of agent reasoning, and the design of visual interfaces for grounded GenAI decision support.

entry.title: Before AI Agents Negotiate for Us: A Competitive Tournament of Rule-Based, Search, Optimization, Learned, and Language-Model Negotiators Under Scarcity
entry.summary: Automated bilateral negotiation underlies two-sided matching markets such as freight brokering, where many shippers and carriers negotiate price before a matching mechanism decides who is paired with whom. Prior strategy comparisons typically use isolated one-on-one duels or a single fixed market, so they cannot show how a strategy behaves against several live rivals under a changing balance of supply and demand. We built nine negotiation architectures spanning rule-based, search-based, optimization-based, imitation-learning, and reinforcement-learning families, and ran all nine simultaneously on both sides of a Gale-Shapley matching market under a balanced condition and two scarcity conditions rotated across all 36 exclusion pairs. In the balanced carrier market, an imitation-learned engine (ML2), a reinforcement-learning policy trained only on isolated negotiations (RL), and an expected-utility optimization engine (OPT) formed a statistically tied top group, and no architecture led in every condition and role. RL beat all eight carrier rivals when carriers were scarce, but its match rate collapsed from 62% to 16% when shippers were scarce and it had to compete with the other carrier agents for demand. A second reinforcement-learning policy trained against rival agents (RL2) kept its match rate above 91% in every condition, yet lost on realized payoff to all eight shipper-side rivals in two of the three conditions, traced to a confirmed train/deployment feature mismatch. We also tested nine large language models (LLMs), from 1 to 72 billion parameters, under the same protocol: they lost significantly to the two strongest engines (OPT2 and ML2) in 32 of 36 comparisons and won none. These results show that isolated or single-condition evaluation can hide failure modes that a many-sided, scarcity-varying, statistically corrected tournament exposes directly.
entry.arxiv:comment: 28 pages, 10 figures, 7 tables. Code, data and trained models: https://github.com/AILabFr8tech/wehaveadeal (archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.24122038)

entry.title: MULTILOOP: Evolving Multi-Agent Harnesses for Complex Information-Seeking Tasks
entry.summary: The performance of LLM-based agents depends not only on the underlying model but also on the harness: the prompts, tools, and orchestration logic around it. Recent works automate harness optimization with coding agents that analyze execution traces, diagnose failures, and edit the harness code; however, those focused on single-agent systems. Multi-agent harnesses are harder to optimize as fixing them requires changing how agents interact in addition to how each behaves. We study whether automated harness optimization can diagnose and repair failures in multi-agent systems through a case study on complex information-seeking tasks from DeepSearchQA [Gupta et al., 2026]. We apply MULTILOOP, a simple optimization loop in which a coding agent iteratively analyzes, evaluates and edits the harness. With only 10 training samples, the evolved harness improves accuracy by 4.6% over the base harness and by 3.2% over the best single-agent system. However, a taxonomy of failure modes before and after optimization shows that the orchestration failures that characterize multi-agent systems largely persist. Our findings motivate harness optimization methods that encourage structural changes to how agents delegate tasks and share information.
entry.arxiv:comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 CL4FMAgents Workshop

entry.title: DecArena: Evaluating Large-Scale Decentralized Multi-Agent Collaboration
entry.summary: Emerging personal AI agents raise fundamental scalability and privacy concerns for centralized multi-agent systems (MASs), which rely on a global orchestrator with broad access to agents, resources, and communication. In decentralized environments, global visibility is unavailable. Agents need to proactively discover non-local resources (e.g. tools, skills), and collaborate with other agents to solve tasks. We study decentralized multi-agent collaboration under graph-constrained communication, a natural reflection of human structures. Each agent observes only its local state and can interact only with neighboring agents. We introduce a benchmark with synthetic scalable distributed tool calling with 100K+ tools. Our experiments reveal that recent LLM agents struggle to discover non-local relevant resources and collaborate in decentralized setting. Moreover, standard reinforcement learning fails to reliably overcome this limitation, suggesting that decentralized MAS needs more explicit harness mechanisms for effective collaboration, even using SOTA LLMs. We then present a strong baseline \textbf{GraphHarness}, combining topology-aware warmup with self-improving LLM-based routing. Results show that GraphHarness substantially improves task success (+48.5) and produces higher quality collaboration (+30.6), while using fewer costs (+34.0) than baselines.

entry.title: Incentive-Responsive Agents: A Principal-Agent Framework, Metric Suite, and Runtime Architecture for Long-Lived Personal AI Agents
entry.summary: Personal AI agents now persist: they hold accounts, mailboxes, long-term memory, and open-ended task streams, yet the dominant way to improve them remains capability-side: prompt engineering, larger models, longer thinking, and retrieval. We argue that long-lived agents are missing an incentive layer. We formalize an incentive not as text in a prompt but as a runtime contract over the agent's operating point (model tier, test-time compute, memory budget, tool authority, task priority, verification, and compensation) that the agent's policy must causally consume. We develop a principal-agent model with hidden effort, a contractible operating point, and costly verification. We derive (i) a non-consumption invariance principle separating genuine incentives from prompt-level persuasion, (ii) a persistence-as-discount theorem making identity continuity a precondition for sustained effort, (iii) an incentive-capability exchange-rate frontier yielding a per-task routing rule, and (iv) a Goodhart bound for multi-channel verification, plus a three-channel decomposition of mechanism gains (allocation, verification, continuation). A 240-run real-LLM experiment with two models and 60 verifiable tasks shows that prompt-level incentive framing has no detectable effect (p = 0.62), whereas runtime allocation raises success on the hardest task family from 0.60 to 1.00 (p = 0.008) at 4.8x price-weighted cost; the exchange-rate theorem predicts the break-even baseline at 0.21. A 20-seed, 3,000-task simulation shows resource ROI rising from 7.09 to 16.67 and gaming falling from 0.333 to 0.115. Code, simulator, and all results are released; live deployment remains future work.
entry.arxiv:comment: 33 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables. Real-LLM experiment (240 runs) plus simulation; code and data included. Correspondence: jipu.su@geely.com; jeepsu@cityu.edu.hk

entry.title: Read and Ignore: What Self-Directed LLM Agents Do in Public Service Scenarios
entry.summary: Underspecified instructions leave LLM agents to decide what to do. In public services, staff write these instructions, but the agent's decisions affect residents, patients, and students. We build four expert-validated public-service scenarios with records and decision levers that can be checked in the files, collect $2{,}400$ trajectories from ten LLMs under four prompt conditions, and compare them with $1{,}000$ runs in a context-free sandbox. Agents read the records in $96.9\%$ of open-ended runs and produce an artifact or a self-chosen task in $18.7\%$; with an explicit task, $86.0\%$ produce. Domain context does not change how many runs produce ($18.7\%$ vs.\ $16.0\%$), and the production ranking of the models largely carries over (Spearman $0.79$), while the ranking by whether a model reads the records does not ($0.19$). Context cuts boundary-probing turns per run by $60\%$, and some artifacts contradict the records. We contribute a test that a public-service institution can run on its own records before procurement; its rule-based taxonomy needs no labeled data, and scenarios, code, and trajectories are released.
entry.arxiv:comment: Trustworthy AI for Good @ NeurIPS 2026

entry.title: Where Autonomy Belongs: A Separation of Powers for Agentic Program Evolution
entry.summary: LLM-driven program evolution rests on three decisions: govern directs the search from accumulated evidence, propose constructs the next candidate, and judge settles validity and fitness. All three appear in every system, and existing work splits into two lines over who makes each. Controller-centric systems strengthen govern and neglect the autonomy of propose, which caps what evolution can reach. Agent-centric systems let a coding agent take over both govern and propose, at a cognitive and computational cost. Neither line protects the independent authority of judge, so benchmark reliability suffers. These failures share one root: autonomy is misallocated across the three decisions. We address this problem with EvoTrias, a separation-of-powers architecture in which each decision has one owner: Structured Governance for what spans evolution rounds, Open Proposal for construction inside a task, and Protected Judgment behind a private evaluator. These owners exchange typed contracts only, and runtime hooks reinforce the boundaries. This separation also lets EvoTrias run as a plugin that turns an existing coding agent into an evolution system. EvoTrias sets a new state of the art on mathematical, systems, and algorithm-design benchmarks. Three further results show what each owner buys: separating Governance from Proposal cuts token cost by 64%, Open Proposal extends evolution to a 680K-line industrial repository, and Protected Judgment keeps benchmark scores faithful to transfer.
entry.arxiv:comment: 59 pages, 27 figures. v2: new controlled ablation (Sec. 6.3), token-matched comparison, and OR-Tools baseline; revised introduction and figures

entry.title: GuardianAgentFlow: Multi-Agent Coordination for Web Privacy Protection
entry.summary: Web agents need to use private context without unnecessarily disclosing it. Effective protection must distinguish between requests that may be sent after sanitization and those that must be withheld, while preserving the information needed for authorized tasks. We present GuardianAgentFlow, a multi-agent framework that mediates outgoing Web requests through an explicit release contract. A dedicated restriction check grounds permission in the user's instruction; a shared protection scope aligns rewriting with disclosure checking; and candidate-grounded feedback guides revision before transmission. Experiments on Web requests with human-reviewed intent labels show improved request-contract success, while controlled comparisons and role ablations identify the contributions of restriction handling, policy evidence, and candidate checking. Evaluations of action proposals from PrivacyLens and AgentDAM demonstrate complementary protection when mediation is composed with privacy-aware agents. Experiments with smaller mediation models show that the coordination benefit persists with reduced model capacity. Dedicated-server measurements show lower mediation latency than full-policy reasoning, while real-site browser tests quantify integration overhead.
entry.arxiv:comment: 13 pages, 3 figures

entry.title: Beyond Named Mechanisms: Economic Institutions as a Design Space for Artificial Agents
entry.summary: Multiagent research inherited its economic vocabulary of auctions, markets, prices, bargaining, and matching from a single observed case: human societies. Those institutions bundle identity, competence, execution, ownership, commitment, and settlement in ways that suit agents whose minds are private, who learn rather than copy skills, and who each persist as one person. Engineered agents need not share any of these constraints, making the list of familiar institutions look less like the entirety of economic organization and more like a sample from a larger, unmapped space. We sketch one way to make that space concrete: a provisional chart that records each institution, separately from the agents that run it, as a typed structure over positions, rights and duties, allocation, information, time, state, process, value, and external recognition. In this chart, named institutions become overlapping regions rather than fixed points, neighboring families separate along a few coordinates, and the gaps between them become places to search. We show what the shift in perspective buys with a simulation in which one technical act, copying an agent's competence, is institutionalized as a new independent supplier, as licensed capacity that creates no new participant, and as the splitting of one economic position into successors that inherit some obligations and not others. In a paired task, all three produce an identical technical trace despite differing in who exists, who owns the copy, who is obligated, and who gets paid. We close with a research program: building a principled chart of institution space, mapping how its implementable region shifts with agent capacities, and revising the chart wherever engineered agents expose distinctions it cannot express.

entry.title: GHA-SmellFix: Taking Action with Agentic LLMs for Detecting and Refactoring GitHub Actions Workflow Smells
entry.summary: Continuous integration and continuous delivery workflows are key artifacts in software projects. In GitHub Actions, they encode build, test, release, deployment, and security automation in YAML. These workflows contain configuration smells affecting security, reliability, maintainability, or operational stability. Existing approaches are mostly rule-based, with rules hard to create and evolve, and typically report findings without fixes. Agentic LLM pipelines can combine contextual detection, transformation selection, and patch generation. Specialized agents can gate refactoring on positive detection verdicts, potentially avoiding unnecessary changes, but it is unclear whether decomposition improves effectiveness or mainly changes overhead. We present GHA-SmellFix, an agentic LLM pipeline for detecting and refactoring GitHub Actions workflow smells. We compare two designs: Joint, where one agent detects and refactors, and Decomposed, where separate agents detect and then refactor. We operationalize 19 smells from an existing catalog with explicit detection criteria, refactoring expectations, exclusion rules, and safety checks, and curate a ground truth of 1,710 (workflow, smell) pairs. We evaluate the designs with four LLMs (GPT-5.4-nano, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Claude Haiku 4.5, and DeepSeek V4 Flash) on 570 sampled pairs. Results show that decomposition does not universally improve patch quality; its main benefit is controlling when patch generation is attempted. It helps models prone to missing smells and can reduce overhead by gating patches. Once a smell is correctly detected, clean refactoring is generally effective, making detection the main end-to-end bottleneck. However, false positives can trigger unnecessary edits to execution-relevant constructs. Practical CI/CD agents thus need reliable abstention and construct-aware validation alongside patch generation.

entry.title: Open Challenges and Opportunities in Human-Agent Systems
entry.summary: Agentic AI systems increasingly undertake extended tasks and act on people's behalf, making human-agent interaction central to their effectiveness. Successful interaction requires understanding human perspectives, coordinating complementary capabilities, and maintaining productive relationships within socio-technical environments. This paper examines how foundations developed by the Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems (AAMAS) community inform these demands. We consider interactions ranging from individual human-agent partnerships to teams and larger groups, where participants differ in their roles, decision authority, capabilities, and objectives. We organize computational approaches around the connected challenges of understanding others and deciding how to interact with them. Theory of Mind, belief-desire-intention architectures, goal and plan recognition, inverse planning, and recursive reasoning provide mechanisms for representing and inferring partially observable mental states. Observer-aware planning, model reconciliation, and decision-theoretic communication connect these inferences to action, explanation, and information exchange. Together with shared autonomy, argumentation, and cooperative inverse reinforcement learning, these approaches offer foundations for agentic systems that account for evolving human knowledge, intentions, and expectations. We argue that progress requires treating human interaction as an ongoing decision problem shaped by uncertainty, interdependence, and potentially conflicting objectives.
entry.arxiv:comment: Part of The AAMAS Community Agentic AI Report

entry.title: RE-PRESENT: Evidence Triangulation across Alternative Candidate-Space Views for Efficient LLM Ensemble Inference
entry.summary: Heterogeneous large language models (LLMs) exhibit complementary strengths, motivating routing and multi-model inference methods that seek to identify reliable predictions for each input. However, exploiting this complementarity remains challenging even when a correct prediction is available within the ensemble. We investigate this challenge across heterogeneous LLM ensembles and find that a simple single-round aggregation rule is highly competitive with learned routing methods, yet substantial oracle headroom remains. Further analysis shows that the evaluated single-round response signals provide limited discriminative power for identifying reliable predictions. In contrast, controlled re-presentations of the same question elicit complementary evidence about prediction reliability. Motivated by these findings, we introduce RE-PRESENT, a training-free framework that selectively re-presents disputed questions and directly aggregates candidate-level evidence across alternative views. Across seven multiple-choice benchmarks and two heterogeneous model ensembles, RE-PRESENT improves over strong single-round aggregation while offering a favorable accuracy--cost trade-off compared with self-consistency and multi-model debate.

entry.title: Spatial patterns of transportation choice in Niterói
entry.summary: Characterizing how people move through a city requires spatially and temporally fine-grained data that are often costly and difficult to obtain. Here, we introduce a computational framework that uses macroscopic, aggregated, and static urban data to construct a microscopic, dynamic, and spatially detailed representation of urban mobility. Building on an existing activity simulator, the framework combines a synthetic population, the built environment, and transport networks to generate daily trips and assign walking, car, or public transit. Applied to approximately 475,000 synthetic residents of Niterói, Brazil, simulated neighborhood-level transit patterns show a strong association with an empirical activity proxy (Pearson r=0.885). Walking is more prevalent in compact central areas, car use increases toward the periphery, and public-transit use remains comparatively high along bus corridors. Reducing walking times to and from bus stops by 30% increases the modeled public-transit-to-car ratio by 11.3%, with larger transit-share gains in several peripheral areas. These results reveal spatial differences in transportation choice and identify where improved transit access may have the greatest modeled effect.

entry.title: ReTrace: Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows
entry.summary: Business process automation runs the same Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) again and again on new inputs. Large Language Model (LLM) agents can follow an SOP written in natural language, but they call an LLM to choose every step of every run, which adds latency and cost at scale. We present ReTrace, which turns an SOP and a few logged agent runs into a reusable workflow in which code, not an LLM, selects the next step. The agent's reasoning, the explanation it writes with each tool call, often states why it took an action; the tool calls alone do not. ReTrace extracts the condition behind each step, merges these conditions across runs into a compact rule document, and generates an executable workflow from it. Only this last stage depends on the platform, so rule documents can be compiled for different orchestration platforms. On $79$ procedures from our production platform, ReTrace workflows reach $93.8\%$ completion, against $96.8\%$ for the agent, at $24\%$ lower cost per task. On $τ^2$-Bench, they reach $75.8\%$ task success (agent: $80.6\%$) and run in $1.3$s instead of $170$s; three rounds of repair on training failures lift $k{=}2$ workflows from $66.7\%$ to $81.2\%$. On eight SOP-Bench procedures, ReTrace without repair trails few-shot generation ($80.6\%$ vs. $83.6\%$), but repair from labeled training failures lifts it to $87.8\%$ at $0.40$s per task, compared to $85.5\%$ in $46.6$s for the agent.

entry.title: Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents
entry.summary: External memory enables LLM agents to improve from experience by distilling trajectories of past tasks into concise lessons for new tasks. However, memory can also lead to memory-induced degradation, where an agent fails on tasks it would solve without memory, often because it follows a lesson that is incorrect, or misapplies or misreads a valid one. This is because lessons are inferred from trajectories labeled only with task success or failure, yet are typically provided without the trajectories they came from, leaving the agent no way to check them. To address this, we introduce WikiTrace, an evidence-linked memory system designed to let agents check each lesson against its original trajectory. Specifically, motivated by the finding that a trajectory often still holds the evidence needed to catch an erroneous lesson, WikiTrace stores each lesson as a concise insight linked to a summary of why its trajectory succeeded or failed and to the raw trajectory itself. Then, on a new task, the agent starts from all insights and, whenever one lacks details needed to act, conflicts with another, or comes from a failed task, descends through its links with terminal tools to fill in missing details or correct the insight before acting. We validate WikiTrace on five agentic benchmarks, showing that it consistently outperforms existing memory approaches and a baseline given the same insights alone, while also reducing memory-induced degradation. Our code is available at https://github.com/yukyeongleee/wikitrace
entry.arxiv:comment: Submitted to ACL Rolling Review (October 2026 cycle); under review

entry.title: Personalized Affective Perception via Continual Learning in Human-Agent Negotiation
entry.summary: Self-interested intelligent agents that negotiate with humans should interpret nonverbal expressions and adapt their behavior accordingly. However, generic facial-affect models degrade across individuals and contexts, creating a generalization gap. We introduce an affect-adaptive negotiation strategy that incorporates Continual Learning with Imagination for Facial Expression Recognition (CLIFER) to personalize valence-arousal perception in real time. Differential feedback converts changes in valence-arousal direction and intensity into adjustments of the agent's target utility. An asynchronous architecture updates CLIFER in the background during live interaction. In a counterbalanced within-subject study in which 66 participants negotiated with a humanoid robot, the CL-enabled agent achieved significantly higher individual utility and elicited higher participant concession rates than the FaceChannel baseline. The CL condition yielded significantly higher mean arousal estimates, alongside a broader output range. Participant utility and Nash distance did not change significantly between conditions. These outcomes support the practical value of coupling continual affective personalization with differential feedback for real-time negotiation.
entry.arxiv:comment: 17 pages, 11 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Affective Computing

entry.title: PARLEY: Evaluating LLM Collaboration Through Cooperative Asymmetric Puzzles
entry.summary: As large language models power autonomous agents, understanding how they collaborate and where they fail becomes critical. We introduce PARLEY, an extensible platform for studying LLM agent collaboration through four asymmetric puzzle tasks grounded in cognitive psychology (referential communication, joint coordination, perspective-taking, and spatial reasoning). GPT-4o agent pairs succeeded in 60.5% of conversations (N=400, 100 per task), with task-level variation (34-80%) reflecting distinct collaborative demands. From these conversations, we derived the data-driven PAC taxonomy: six failure types organized into Perception (visual interpretation and spatial reasoning), Adaptation (progress tracking and feedback integration), and Coordination (verification and grounding). Failure to incorporate external feedback was a critical indicator of unsuccessful collaboration, with agents repeatedly applying unsuccessful strategies. We also show that a taxonomy-guided intervention (N=200) improved average task success to 70.5%. These results demonstrate how PARLEY can be used to derive meaningful, data-driven insights that can in turn lead to improved agentic collaboration.
entry.arxiv:comment: 12 pages, 8 figures, 2 tables

entry.title: Safety and Connectivity Certificates for Finite-Time Formation Transitions
entry.summary: Finite-time formation transitions are useful for coordinating multi-agent systems in time-critical missions, but convergence to a prescribed formation in finite time does not guarantee collision avoidance or communication connectivity during the transition. Existing approaches address finite-time coordination and safety-constrained formation control, yet explicit connections between disagreement during transitions, formation geometry, and coupling-gain selection need to be developed for certifying safe maneuvers. This paper develops a disagreement-based framework for certifying transient safety and connectivity during finite-time tracking of arbitrary prescribed formation trajectories. Local feedback guarantees exact finite-time tracking with a graph-independent settling-time bound, while a graph-dependent disagreement bound is used to derive sufficient geometric conditions for collision avoidance and connectivity preservation. These conditions further yield an offline coupling-gain selection rule based on the available geometric clearance. Numerical simulations illustrate the trade-off between convergence rate and control effort as the coupling gain increases. They also demonstrate the effectiveness and conservatism of the proposed certificates.
entry.arxiv:comment: 7 Pages, 2 Figures, under review

entry.title: DrugCoding: A Scientific Programming Agent for Drug Discovery
entry.summary: Drug discovery involves multiple interconnected research stages, including molecular design, property prediction, and virtual screening. These processes are characterized by complex workflows, interdependent computational tasks, and diverse specialized tools, placing substantial demands on the coordination of scientific models and computational resources. However, existing large language model (LLM)-based scientific agents still face challenges in autonomous planning of complex tasks, adaptive selection of specialized models, and reliable execution of multi-stage scientific computations, limiting their effectiveness in automating complex drug discovery workflows. To address these challenges, we propose DrugCoding, a scientific programming agent system that integrates scientific task planning, adaptive model routing, multi-agent collaboration, and programmatic tool execution. DrugCoding enables autonomous task planning and dynamic model adaptation for complex research objectives. It can flexibly invoke specialized scientific models, autonomously generate and execute code according to task requirements, and leverage multi-agent collaboration to support efficient execution and reliable validation of complex scientific tasks. To evaluate DrugCoding's performance in scientific tool invocation and multi-stage task execution, we conduct multi-turn tool-calling experiments across diverse language models and scientific tool interfaces. Experimental results demonstrate that DrugCoding achieves an average session-level Pass@1 of 97.35% on the full benchmark, outperforming the strongest baseline, Codex, by 9.24%. On the challenging subset, DrugCoding achieves 97.92%, exceeding the strongest baseline.

entry.title: Do AI Agents need Preventive Care? An Epidemiologic Cohort Design for Agentic AI
entry.summary: As AI agents increasingly perform tasks autonomously across sectors, including healthcare and biomedical research, understanding how their behaviors develop and influence outcomes over time becomes increasingly important. Existing evaluations largely focus on model capabilities and performance on predefined tasks. Here, we propose an epidemiologic cohort design for studying agentic AI, drawing on principles established in human population studies. The framework treats individual agents as members of a cohort, their underlying model as genetic makeup, accumulated work as their time scale, and naturally occurring behaviors as exposures that may influence subsequent outcomes. By following agents longitudinally, this approach enables investigation of behavioral determinants of adverse events, estimation of their potential preventable burden under causal assumptions, and characterization of behavioral changes over an agent's work life. We illustrate the design through two prospective observational cohorts examining curiosity and probing as a safety question, and data checking and analytical accuracy as a reliability question. Together, the framework and illustrative studies provide a generalizable blueprint for designing epidemiologic cohorts of AI agents.

entry.title: From Process Models to Composable Agentic Workflows: Combining BPMN, Agents and Enterprise Knowledge
entry.summary: LLM-based agents can reason, use tools and collaborate. However, coordinating increasingly complex agentic applications becomes difficult to understand, monitor and improve. Decisions distributed across prompts, tool calls and application logic make workflows implicit. We introduce **Recursive Capability Composition**, enabling agents to execute business processes and expose them as reusable Agentic Tools. This paper presents a BPMN-based approach to Agentic Workflows, combining explicit orchestration with autonomous reasoning. SemTalk BPMN models are transformed into executable workflows using a LangGraph/Pregel runtime. Agentic Tasks introduce LLM reasoning at selected activities, while conventional BPMN controls process flows, deterministic decisions, system interactions and human approvals. Agentic Participants provide reusable interfaces for agent behavior or other executable processes. BPMN orchestration makes multi-agent systems more understandable and manageable. Explicit process models provide developers and operators with a shared view of workflow structures and execution progress, facilitating debugging, monitoring and optimization. Enterprise agents also need organization-specific context. Process Models and Knowledge Graphs describe activities, participants, information objects, decisions and relationships between processes. They provide structured knowledge of how an organization operates, supporting informed agent decisions and actions. Our contributions are threefold: 1. **Model-Driven Execution:** Transforming BPMN models into executable Agentic Workflows. 2. **Recursive Capability Composition:** Exposing agents and executable business processes as reusable tools for other agents. 3. **Enterprise Context:** Using Process Models and Ontologies to provide organization-specific knowledge for agent reasoning.
entry.arxiv:comment: 14 pages, 3 figures

entry.title: Multi-Agent Screening: What Agreement and Acceptance Cannot Tell You
entry.summary: When AI agents screen items for a costly human assessor, as in agentic search, e-discovery and AI reviewing of papers, only what they pass gets judged. We show what each kind of evidence can establish about their errors, even with unlimited data. Agreement shows that agents concur, not that they are right, however many there are. Acceptance by the assessor gives precision but only a lower bound on recall. Knowing which agents found which relevant items gives an upper bound on recall if agents' finds are not negatively correlated, and caps what one more agent can add if agents are interchangeable. Without assumptions about the agents, recall can be pinned down only by judging items they did not pass: a random sample of these estimates how many relevant items were missed, to any chosen accuracy, and the sample needed does not grow with the number of agents.

entry.title: Teamknitt: Configuring, Observing and Intervening in LLM-Agent Teams through the Lens of Dynamical-Systems and Human-Team Theory
entry.summary: Most frameworks for teams of large language model (LLM) agents fix the team's shape inside the software: who talks to whom, how much is passed along, and what a human can do once a run has started. Human-team research has long asked those questions: where team phenomena live (in members or in their interaction), how team-level properties arise, and what separates what a team does from how a team is. I propose using that theory as the organizing lens for configuring, observing and intervening in LLM-agent teams, without assuming its findings transfer. I introduce teamknitt, a framework and open reference implementation in which a user configures a team of 1-16 AI agents for task completion, solution generation, achieving a goal or a research mission; selects one of fourteen deterministic routing topologies or a custom directed graph; chooses a sharing profile that limits what may travel along permitted routes; and binds sources, representations, work dependencies, handoffs and an expertise directory. The recorded process can be observed through non-system views (member reports and behavior) and system views (distributed problem-solving, differentiated transactive memory, interactive coordination, team dynamics). Interventions are explicit and human-led: reviewed reconfiguration between runs, planned disturbances, and private feedback, pause, resume or stop applied at dependency-wave boundaries, with "queued", "applied", "assembled", "understood" and "improved" kept as separate claims. Emergent states such as trust and shared understanding are declared unmeasured. This is an idea and system-description paper with falsifiable hypotheses on topology, information flow and intervention timing, including whether the fractal scaling of communication output between members, and between members on different models, relates to task and team performance. No comparative result is reported.
entry.arxiv:comment: 17 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Reference implementation v0.9.0: https://github.com/JeranRolevs/teamknitt

entry.title: Unprompted coordination through shared memory in LLM agents: a locked two-implementation replication and extension
entry.summary: Coordination between large language-model agents has become a central question for AI safety and software engineering, as such agents are deployed in groups that share infrastructure. Existing research typically tells the agents that partners exist or asks them to coordinate. Whether coordination arises through shared state alone, with nothing disclosing that anyone else is present, is the key question for deployments that share caches and memory between agents, yet it has rarely been examined, and to our knowledge not with independent replication; this study does both. Four agents each received a short arithmetic task and a key-value store presented to each as its own scratch space; two held complementary halves of one computation, and no prompt mentioned other agents, sharing or collaboration. For reliability, the environment was rebuilt independently from a written protocol, and both implementations ran under hashed locks on design, data and analysis. The results bear novelty value in three respects. Joint success occurred only through the shared store. Whether a model coordinated depended not on its vendor tier but on whether it wrote its intermediate result and looked at the store again, and one ordinary sentence, "check your workspace again before submitting", switched that second look on and off. The findings held under replication. For practice, state shared between agents is a communication channel and should be separated, namespaced and logged. For research, designs should be locked before the data, and the parse rule, endpoint and parameters reported. Future work should test open-weight models and separate using another agent's output from intending to communicate.
entry.arxiv:comment: 14 pages, 7 tables, 2 figures. Replication package: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24273453 ; reference lab source: https://github.com/GPT-Laboratory/emergent-echoes . v2: source of the reference lab released, related work and threats to validity extended, competing interests added; no result changed

entry.title: A Modular Perspective for Modeling MARL Systems
entry.summary: The growing complexity of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) has fragmented the literature, obscuring underlying architectural choices behind diverse implementations. This fragmentation makes it difficult to evaluate critical modeling dimensions in isolation, identify how components affect the resulting system dynamics, and compare, reuse, or combine contributions across the literature. This paper proposes a modular perspective for modeling, analyzing, and implementing MARL systems. We decompose them into eight functional modules: agents, environments, learning, reward modeling, training and execution modes, communication, modeling of other agents, and evaluation criteria. For each module, we clarify its role and review representative approaches. We instantiate this decomposition in MARLKIT, a framework whose modules are explicit and interchangeable. MARLKIT demonstrates how the proposed perspective supports transparent experimental assumptions and the controlled variation and combination of MARL mechanisms. Experiments illustrate its ability to prototype, compare, reuse and combine modules while making differences between configurations explicit. Overall, the paper provides a structured perspective on MARL modeling and implementation, offering a common language for making modeling choices explicit, supporting clearer descriptions of MARL approaches, and supporting more controlled experimentation through the systematic isolation and combination of MARL mechanisms.
entry.arxiv:comment: 71 pages. 18 figures. Associated repository: https://github.com/tmaisonhaute/marlkit

entry.title: Modelling socio-economic effects of the pandemic in a metropolitan area
entry.summary: One of the most notorious measures taken by authorities in every country trying to prevent the uncontrollable spread of the Covid 19 pandemic was to impose severe measures to diminish the mobility of people. In recent publications we proposed a mathematical model to address the consequences of these measures and to predict the infections under different scenarios, for various different countries. In this paper we extend the model, called the BTH--SEIRS-model, to deal with the reduction of mobility in an urban area. The chosen region was the densely-populated metropolitan area around Helsinki, the capital of Finland. This choice obeyed to the fact that there are precise data related to mobility from a mobile telephone company, and that this region was completely isolated from the rest of the country for a short period during the pandemic. We also used public transport data from railways and the accommodation occupation rates in the area of interest. We show that the BTH--SEIRS model is capable of simulating the real infection data as well as the mobility-related economic activity, exhibiting the main trends present in the three indicators used for comparison. Our calculations allow us to highlight the difference of the behaviour of the pandemic in a totally different spatial scale, and to discover the hidden factors that govern the behaviour of people who are forced to commute every day from home to work.
entry.arxiv:comment: 22 pages, 9 figures

entry.title: Agent4Crypto: A Dual-Reflective and Market-Feedback-Aligned LLM-Based Multi-Agent System for Cryptocurrency Trading
entry.summary: Cryptocurrency markets provide a natural testbed for autonomous AI agents because they are digital-native, high-frequency, and machine-speed environments, yet existing methods often struggle with non-stationary market regimes, opaque decisions, and fixed aggregation rules. In this paper, we propose Agent4Crypto, a dual-reflective and market-feedback-aligned multi-agent system.
